creeds.name: The rule of faith (Irenaeus and Tertullian)

date.display: c. 180 AD (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.10.1) and about 200 AD (Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics 13)

creeds.occasion: Before any council wrote a creed, teachers summed up the faith that the churches had received from the apostles. Irenaeus and Tertullian set these summaries against teachers who claimed a secret tradition of their own. Tertullian calls it the rule of faith. The later baptismal creeds grew from summaries like these.
creeds.held_note: Not a fixed text that any church adopts as its creed; it is the shared summary the later creeds grew from.
creeds.key_text: The Church, though dispersed throughout the whole world, even to the ends of the earth, has received from the apostles and their disciples this faith: [She believes] in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them; and in one Christ Jesus, the Son of God, who became incarnate for our salvation; and in the Holy Spirit, who proclaimed through the prophets

extra_excerpts.text: there is one only God, and that He is none other than the Creator of the world, who produced all things out of nothing through His own Word

creeds.name: Council of Ephesus (Mary as Theotokos, Mother of God)
creeds.occasion: Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, preferred to call Mary Christotokos (Christ-bearer) rather than Theotokos (God-bearer), to guard the full humanity of Christ. Cyril of Alexandria held that the one born of Mary is God the Word made flesh. The council, opened by Cyril before John of Antioch and the Eastern bishops arrived, approved Cyril's letter; the two sides were reconciled in the Formula of Reunion of 433. It wrote no new creed.

held_by.note: Third ecumenical council.

creeds.name: Definition of Chalcedon
creeds.occasion: After Eutyches taught that Christ's humanity was absorbed into one nature, the council, drawing on the Tome of Pope Leo, confessed one Christ 'in two natures' without confusion or division. Churches of Egypt, Syria and Armenia did not accept its wording, holding to Cyril's 'one nature of the Word incarnate'; this became the largest lasting division of the early church. They saw the two-natures wording as leaning toward Nestorius, and they honour Dioscorus, whom the council deposed.

held_by.note: They reject the council but also reject Eutyches. They call their teaching Miaphysite (one united nature); the WCC calls the old label 'Monophysite' erroneous.
Its own dyophysite (two-nature) Christology follows Theodore of Mopsuestia (GEDSH).

creeds.key_text: the peculiar property of each nature being preserved and being united in one Person and subsistence, not separated or divided into two persons
creeds.key_text_note: The better-known phrase 'in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably' sits in the same sentence but is broken by footnote and page markers in the CCEL text, so a clean adjacent span was used.

creeds.name: The Filioque ('and the Son') in the Western Nicene Creed

date.display: 589 (Third Council of Toledo, as traditionally dated) to 1014 (sung at Mass in Rome); defined as doctrine at Lateran IV (1215), Lyon II (1274) and Florence (1439)

creeds.place: Toledo, Spain; then Frankish lands; then Rome
creeds.occasion: At Toledo III (589, as traditionally dated) the Visigoths, newly turned from Arianism, professed the creed with 'and the Son' added to the procession of the Spirit, to stress the Son's full equality with the Father. The addition spread through Frankish lands. After the Frankish council of Aachen (809), Pope Leo III accepted the teaching but declined to add the words to the creed; the creed with the addition was sung at Mass in Rome from about 1014. The Orthodox hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and that no council may change the creed. The question became one of the issues behind the estrangement of East and West, marked by the excommunications of 1054.

held_by.note: Inherited in the Western creed text.

creeds.name: Third Council of Constantinople (two wills in Christ)
creeds.place: Constantinople (domed hall of the imperial palace)
creeds.occasion: Monothelites taught that Christ had only one will. The council, following the letter of Pope Agatho, confessed two natural wills and two natural operations in Christ, the human will freely following the divine. It also condemned earlier leaders who had backed the one-will teaching, among them Pope Honorius I.

held_by.note: Sixth ecumenical council.

date.display: Latin 1563 (Convocation of "1562", old-style year); English text 1571

creeds.occasion: Under Elizabeth I the Church of England revised Cranmer's Forty-two Articles (1553) to set its position between Rome and the Anabaptists and other radical reformers. Convocation ratified them in 1563; the English text was settled and subscription required in 1571.

held_by.note: Printed in the Book of Common Prayer; weight given to them varies across Anglican provinces (not verified per province).
Wesley abridged them into the Methodist Articles of Religion (1784).

creeds.key_text: We are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ by Faith, and not for our own works or deservings

sources.title: Church of England, Book of Common Prayer: Articles of Religion
sources.supports: Title: Convocation holden at London in the year 1562; ratification by subscription 'in the Year of our Lord 1571'.

sources.title: Philip Schaff, Creeds of Christendom (creeds1.ix.vi.v), CCEL
sources.supports: Convocations of January 1563 reduced the articles to 39, ratified and published 1563; English subscription by the Act of 13 Elizabeth (1571).

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907-1912), 'Calvinism', New Advent
sources.supports: Cranmer and Ridley's 42 Articles of 1553 were reduced to 39 under Elizabeth in 1562.

creeds.name: Book of Concord (with the Formula of Concord)

date.display: Formula completed 1577; Book of Concord published 25 June 1580

creeds.place: Dresden (publication); Formula drafted at Kloster Bergen near Magdeburg
creeds.occasion: After decades of dispute among Luther's heirs, theologians including Jakob Andreae and Martin Chemnitz wrote the Formula of Concord to settle the questions. It was published with the three creeds and the earlier Lutheran confessions as one book on the 50th anniversary of the Augsburg Confession.

held_by.note: The LCMS accepts the Book of Concord of 1580 as binding; some Lutheran churches give primary weight to the Augsburg Confession and Small Catechism.

creeds.key_text: We believe, teach, and confess that the sole rule and standard according to which all dogmas together with [all] teachers should be estimated and judged are the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures of the Old and of the New Testament alone

sources.title: Philip Schaff, Creeds of Christendom (creeds1.viii.vi), CCEL
sources.supports: Formula completed 1577, first published 1580; published at Dresden 25 June 1580, the 50th anniversary of the Augsburg Confession; framers Andreae, Chemnitz, Selnecker, Chytraeus.

sources.title: Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod, "Lutheran Confessions"

creeds.name: Canons of Dort
creeds.occasion: Followers of Jacob Arminius set out five points in the Remonstrance of 1610 (election on foreseen faith, resistible grace, and others). A national synod with foreign Reformed delegates answered them on election, the atonement, grace and perseverance.

held_by.note: Continental Reformed churches (e.g. CRCNA confessions).
Wesleyan Methodism holds the Arminian view that grace is offered to all (WCC Methodist page).

creeds.key_text: Election is God’s unchangeable purpose by which he did the following: Before the foundation of the world, by sheer grace, according to the free good pleasure of his will, God chose in Christ to salvation a definite number of particular people out of the entire human race

sources.title: Christian Reformed Church in North America, Canons of Dort
sources.supports: Synod met at Dordrecht 1618-19 with 26 delegates from 8 foreign countries; answered the Remonstrance of 1610.

creeds.name: Dordrecht Confession of Faith (Mennonite)
creeds.occasion: Flemish and Frisian Mennonite preachers adopted 18 articles, first drafted by Adriaan Cornelisz, as a basis of union between divided Mennonite groups. It teaches believers' baptism, foot washing, church discipline and shunning, non-resistance, and refusal of oaths.

held_by.use: confessional for Amish and conservative Mennonites
held_by.note: Adopted in Alsace 1660 and by Pennsylvania Mennonites 1725; still recognized by the Amish (GAMEO, Third Way).

creeds.key_text: we confess with the mouth, and believe with the heart, with all the pious, according to the holy Scriptures, in one eternal, almighty, and incomprehensible God, the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost

creeds.name: Westminster Confession of Faith

date.display: Completed and presented to Parliament 4 December 1646; proof texts 1647; adopted by the Church of Scotland 27 August 1647

creeds.occasion: During the English Civil War, Parliament called an assembly of divines to reform the Church of England, partly to secure an alliance with Scotland. The confession became the doctrinal standard of Presbyterian churches worldwide.

held_by.note: Adopted by the Church of Scotland in 1647; the confessional standard of the Orthodox Presbyterian Church today (OPC site). Other Presbyterian bodies not verified individually.
The Second London Baptist Confession is modelled on it.

creeds.key_text: The authority of the Holy Scripture, for which it ought to be believed, and obeyed, dependeth not upon the testimony of any man, or church; but wholly upon God (who is truth itself) the author thereof

sources.title: Philip Schaff, Creeds of Christendom (creeds1.ix.viii.iii), CCEL
sources.supports: Editio princeps printed (not published) 7 December 1646; second edition with Scripture proofs ordered 29 April 1647; Parliament adopted a revised form.

sources.title: PCA Historical Center, "This Day in Presbyterian History: August 27, Church of Scotland Adopts WCF (1647)"
sources.supports: Church of Scotland adopted the Confession on 27 August 1647.

creeds.name: Second London Baptist Confession ("1689 Confession")

date.display: First published 1677; approved by the first General Assembly of Particular Baptists, 1689

creeds.occasion: Particular (Calvinistic) Baptists modelled a confession on Westminster to show their agreement with other Reformed Protestants, changing it on baptism, church order and the Lord's Supper. After the 1689 Act of Toleration, delegates from over 100 churches approved it openly.

held_by.note: Adopted in America by the Philadelphia Association (1742). Many other Baptists use later confessions or none.

creeds.key_text: The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience

sources.title: Philip Schaff, Creeds of Christendom (creeds1.x.vi), CCEL
sources.supports: Appeared first in 1677 in London; reprinted 1688, 1689; approved by ministers of over a hundred congregations; adopted at Philadelphia 25 Sept 1742.

sources.supports: Published 1677; revised by the first general assembly (over 100 congregations) in 1689; Philadelphia Association 1742.

creeds.name: Methodist Articles of Religion

date.display: 1784 (Christmas Conference, Baltimore): Wesley's 24 articles plus Article XXIII on the rulers of the United States, added by the conference; wording of XXIII revised 1804

creeds.place: Baltimore, Maryland (Christmas Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church)
creeds.occasion: After American independence, John Wesley abridged the Thirty-nine Articles to 24 for the new Methodist Episcopal Church, leaving out Calvinist-leaning and some other articles. The conference itself added an article recognizing the United States.

held_by.note: In the United Methodist Book of Discipline; also historic standard of other Methodist Episcopal descendants (not verified individually).

creeds.key_text: We are accounted righteous before God only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, by faith, and not for our own works or deservings.
creeds.key_text_note: Compare Thirty-nine Articles art. XI, from which it is drawn.

sources.title: Philip Schaff, Creeds of Christendom (creeds1.x.xi), CCEL

creeds.name: First Vatican Council (Dei Filius; Pastor Aeternus)
creeds.occasion: Facing rationalism and the threatened loss of the Papal States, the council taught on faith and reason (Dei Filius) and defined the primacy of the pope and his infallibility when he speaks ex cathedra on faith or morals.

held_by.note: Some who rejected the decree formed the Old Catholic churches.
Papal jurisdiction is a dividing issue (WCC).

creeds.key_text: he possesses, by the divine assistance promised to him in blessed Peter, that infallibility which the divine Redeemer willed his church to enjoy in defining doctrine concerning faith or morals

creeds.name: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths
creeds.occasion: Two years after the Assemblies of God formed, some ministers adopted Oneness teaching: baptism in Jesus' name only, and one God revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit rather than three distinct persons. The General Council adopted a statement that affirmed the Trinity and tongues as the initial sign of Spirit baptism; 156 ministers left and formed Oneness bodies.

held_by.note: The AG says it is 'intended simply as a basis of fellowship' and that 'The Bible is our all-sufficient rule'.

creeds.key_text: The baptism of believers in the Holy Spirit is witnessed by the initial physical sign of speaking with other tongues as the Spirit of God gives them utterance.

creeds.name: Second Vatican Council
creeds.occasion: Pope John XXIII called the council to renew the church's life and to seek Christian unity. Its 16 documents treat the church, revelation, liturgy, ecumenism and the modern world; it called other Christians 'brothers' and opened official dialogues.

creeds.name: Common Christological Declaration (Catholic Church and Assyrian Church of the East)
creeds.occasion: Pope John Paul II and Catholicos-Patriarch Mar Dinkha IV declared that their churches share one faith in Christ, true God and true man, despite the 5th-century split over Nestorius. Each church's way of naming Mary was recognized as a legitimate expression of the same faith.

held_by.note: Assyrian Church of the East (not the separate Ancient Church of the East).

creeds.key_text: the Assyrian Church of the East is praying the Virgin Mary as "the Mother of Christ our God and Saviour". In the light of this same faith the Catholic tradition addresses the Virgin Mary as "the Mother of God" and also as "the Mother of Christ".
